summary.text: For an arbitrary bound \(B\), take \(M=B+6\) and \(n=M!/6\); a decomposition \(n=x+y\) gives \(M!=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\). If \(6x-1\le B\), it divides \(M!\) and hence the prime \(6y+1\), forcing equality, which is impossible modulo \(6\); similarly, if \(6y-1\le B\), then the prime \(6y+1\le M\) divides \(M!\) and hence \(6x-1\), giving the same contradiction, so both prime families are unbounded and therefore infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal S=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
\mathcal T=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of smaller members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is obtained by considering the integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), putting \(y=n-x\), and counting those \(x\) for which all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Thus, if \(a(n)>0\), at least one summand in this finite count is \(1\). Consequently there are integers \(x,y\ge 1\) such that
\[
x+y=n                                                   \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1                 \tag{2}
\]
are all prime. Indeed, the counted value of \(x\) lies in \(1\le x<n\), and with \(y=n-x\) this gives both (1) and \(y\ge1\).

Assume now the conjectural hypothesis
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.              \tag{3}
\]
We prove separately that \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) are unbounded. Since every finite set of natural numbers is bounded, this will prove that both sets are infinite.

First we prove that the Sophie Germain primes are unbounded. Let \(B\) be any natural number. Define
\[
M=B+6,
\qquad
n=\frac{M!}{6}.
\]
Because \(M\ge6\), the integer \(6\) divides \(M!\), so \(n\) is an integer and
\[
6n=M!.                                                   \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, \(M!\ge6!=720\), and in particular \(M!\ge12\). Equation (4) therefore gives \(n\ge2\), so \(n>1\).

By (3), \(a(n)>0\). Apply the witness observation above to obtain positive integers \(x,y\) satisfying (1) and (2). Put
\[
p=6x-1,
\qquad
q=6y+1.
\]
The number \(p\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Indeed, \(p\) is prime by (2), and, since \(x\ge1\), ordinary integer arithmetic gives
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
which is also prime by (2). Thus \(p\in\mathcal S\).

We claim that \(p>B\). Suppose instead that \(p\le B\). Then
\[
p\le B<M=B+6.
\]
Every positive integer at most \(M\) divides \(M!\), so \(p\mid M!\). On the other hand, using (1) and (4), we have the crucial identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
M!&=6n=6(x+y)\\
  &=6x+6y\\
  &=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+q.                                  \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p\mid M!\), equation (5) shows that \(p\mid p+q\). As \(p\mid p\), subtraction gives \(p\mid q\).

But \(q=6y+1\) is prime by (2). A positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself. The divisor \(p\) cannot be \(1\), since \(p\) is itself prime and hence at least \(2\). Therefore \(p=q\). This is impossible: the equality would say
\[
6x-1=6y+1,
\]
whereas the left side is congruent to \(-1\pmod 6\) and the right side is congruent to \(1\pmod 6\). Equivalently, it would imply that a multiple of \(6\) equals \(2\), which cannot occur. This contradiction proves \(p>B\).

We have therefore shown that for every natural number \(B\), there is an element \(p\in\mathcal S\) with \(p>B\). Hence \(\mathcal S\) is unbounded and consequently infinite.

We next prove that the twin primes are unbounded. Again let \(B\) be an arbitrary natural number, and make the same definitions
\[
M=B+6,
\qquad
n=\frac{M!}{6}.
\]
As before, \(M\ge6\), so \(6\mid M!\),
\[
6n=M!,                                                   \tag{6}
\]
and \(n>1\). Hypothesis (3) again produces positive integers \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\) for which all four numbers in (2) are prime.

Set
\[
r=6y-1,
\qquad
q=6y+1,
\qquad
p=6x-1.
\]
Then \(r\) represents a twin-prime pair: \(r\) is prime, and because \(y\ge1\),
\[
r+2=(6y-1)+2=6y+1=q,
\]
which is also prime. Hence \(r\in\mathcal T\).

We claim that \(r>B\). Suppose, to the contrary, that \(r\le B\). Since \(q=r+2\), we obtain
\[
q\le B+2\le B+6=M.                                     \tag{7}
\]
The positive integer \(q\) is therefore at most \(M\), so \(q\mid M!\). As in (5), equations \(x+y=n\) and (6) give
\[
M!=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+q.                                   \tag{8}
\]
Thus \(q\mid p+q\), and since \(q\mid q\), it follows that \(q\mid p\).

The number \(p=6x-1\) is prime. Hence every positive divisor of \(p\) is either \(1\) or \(p\). The divisor \(q\) is itself prime, so \(q\ge2\) and cannot equal \(1\). We must therefore have \(q=p\). Once more this is impossible, because
\[
q=6y+1\equiv1\pmod6,
\qquad
p=6x-1\equiv-1\pmod6.
\]
Thus the supposition \(r\le B\) leads to a contradiction, and consequently \(r>B\).

For every natural number \(B\), we have now found an element \(r\in\mathcal T\) exceeding \(B\). Therefore \(\mathcal T\) is unbounded and hence infinite.

It follows that the assumption \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\) implies both that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
